title: Long-tail cast-on
subtitle: A two-strand foundation that builds the first row and the edge in a single pass.
excerpt: The long-tail cast-on is the default opening for most UK knitting patterns. This deep dive covers the tail length formula, the thumb-and-finger grip, common tension faults, and the k-tbl variant used in German twisted cast-on.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 1 (1886), opening cast-on chapter. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), pp. 24-28, cast-on methods. Craft Yarn Council needle and yarn weight standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-strand cast-on method worked with a tail of yarn and the working end. Produces the first row of loops and a neat, elastic edge in one pass.

The length of yarn measured out before casting on. For the long-tail method, this tail forms half the stitches; the formula tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15 gives a safe length.
Inserting the needle into the back leg of the stitch rather than the front. Twists the stitch on the needle, producing a firmer, slightly tighter fabric.

content.text: The
long-tail cast-on

(abbreviated lt-co) is the foundation edge for the majority of UK knitting patterns. Unlike the cable or knitted-on cast-on, it works two strands simultaneously: the tail over the left thumb forms the body of each stitch, and the working yarn over the left index finger locks it onto the needle. The result is a firm, springy row of loops that look and behave like a worked knit row. Difficulty: beginner, though the first few attempts feel like a conjuring trick.
What you need
One ball of DK yarn (any smooth wool or wool-blend reads the stitch cleanly)
4 mm straight or circular needles
A tape measure for calculating the tail
Calculating the tail
Running short mid-cast-on is the most common frustration. The safe formula for the
cast-on tail

: length in cm = (needle circumference in mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For a 4 mm needle and 40 stitches: (4 x 40) / 10 + 15 = 31 cm. For 100 stitches on the same needle: (4 x 100) / 10 + 15 = 55 cm. Add 10 cm if unsure of your tension.
The cast-on, step by step
Measure and pull out the required tail. Make a slip knot at that point and place it on the needle. This counts as the first stitch.

Hold the needle in your right hand. With your left hand, spread the thumb and index finger apart and catch both strands: tail over the left thumb, working yarn over the index finger. The remaining fingers close around both strands to anchor the tension.
Rotate the thumb towards you so the yarn forms a loop. Insert the needle tip upward through this thumb loop, from below.
Swing the needle over and catch the index-finger strand, drawing it back through the thumb loop.
Slip the thumb loop off and gently tug the tail to snug the new stitch onto the needle. Not too tight: you will need to work into this stitch on the next row.
Re-form the thumb loop and repeat until you have the required number of stitches.
The k-tbl variant
For a firmer, twisted edge, work step 3 by inserting the needle through the back of the thumb loop rather than the front. This is the
knit through the back loop
principle applied at cast-on. The resulting edge is noticeably tighter and more structured. The German twisted cast-on uses exactly this move throughout.
Where you will see it

The long-tail cast-on opens the great majority of hat, scarf, and sweater patterns in UK print publications. Weldon's Practical Knitter uses a near-identical method under the name 'thumb cast-on'. When a pattern says 'cast on' without specifying a method, the long-tail is the safe default.
It is not suited to provisional cast-ons or to mid-row increases. For those, the cable cast-on or knitted-on cast-on works more cleanly.

items.symptom: Running out of tail before finishing
items.cause: Tail measured too short, or tension tighter than expected
items.fix: Use the formula above and add a 10 cm buffer. If you run out, unknit back to the slip knot and start again with a longer tail.

items.symptom: Stitches too tight to work into on the first row
items.cause: Thumb loop snugged down too hard at step 5
items.fix: Cast on over two needles held together, then remove one before the first row. This leaves the stitches slightly looser.

items.symptom: Edge looks loose and loopy on one side
items.cause: Tail and working yarn swapped: tail should be over the thumb, working yarn over the index finger
items.fix: Check your setup at step 2. The tail side (thumb) produces the bottom bar of each stitch; swapping them reverses the structure.

items.symptom: First stitch (slip knot) noticeably larger than the rest
items.cause: The slip knot creates a visible loop that differs from the cast-on stitches
items.fix: On the first row, knit the slip knot through the back loop to tighten it, or count the slip knot as a separate stitch and cast on one fewer with the long-tail method.

items.cause: Normal behaviour on stocking stitch: the first row of plain knit stitches curls
items.fix: This is the fabric structure, not a cast-on fault. Ribbing, garter, or seed stitch worked for the first few rows will prevent curl.
